I'm no conspiracy theorist, but.......

The world's second-largest bank just paid $1.21 billion for AML failures.

Bank of America. October 13, 2026.

FinCEN: $1.2 billion consent order.
OCC: $750 million — the largest penalty in its history.
OFAC: $11.6 million for 475 sanctions violations.

And BofA admitted what regulators rarely hear:
Willful BSA violations.

Here's exactly what broke.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE FAILURE

BofA's transaction monitoring ran on a threshold set by "stakeholder judgment."

Alert groups needed 20 points within 13 months to generate a case.

When internal testing showed groups just below that threshold had higher SAR yields than expected — no one adjusted it.

Investigations were sometimes launched a year after the transactions occurred. The BSA allows 30 days.

The backlog peaked at 200,000 unworked cases.

Over one-third of investigations started only when subpoenas or law enforcement requests arrived.

That's not monitoring. That's reacting.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE NUMBERS

📌 $5 billion+ in suspicious activity — missed or reported late
📌 $1 billion+ linked to national security and priority illicit finance risks
📌 680,000+ negotiable instrument deposits worth $660M+ from two salvage-vehicle auction accounts — compliance recommended offboarding; the business said no
📌 33,300 outgoing wires (~$1 billion) with inaccurate transmittor information — Travel Rule violations
📌 12 foreign correspondent accounts serving 250+ non-bank institutions — zero expected activity files

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THREE LESSONS

1. Monitoring thresholds are a business decision — not a technical one.
If stakeholders set them and no one validates against SAR outcomes, your firm owns the consequences.

2. Compliance recommendations are not advisory.
BofA was told to offboard high-risk customers. The business declined. The penalty was $1.21 billion.

3. Willful doesn't require intent to commit crime.
It means you knew about deficiencies and failed to fix them. BofA had an OCC cease-and-desist since December 2024. The pattern continued.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

When did your institution last validate its monitoring thresholds against actual SAR outcomes?

Drop your answer below 👇

From one of the country’s first IBM PC labs at Florida Atlantic University to 13+ bosses in my final chapter—after 40+ years in technology, it’s official: I’ve RETIRED.

What a ride it has been since those early days at FAU. Looking back from managing a 400-node network at CIGNA, to building global testing organizations at Bank of America, to leading IT Quality at Ahold Delhaize USA, one truth has stayed constant: change isn't just something that happens in this industry. Change IS the industry.

Through countless mergers, reorganizations, operating models, and more acronyms than anyone should reasonably be expected to remember, what always impressed me most wasn't the technology. It was the heart of the people.

When I reflect on what we built across the US, India, Mexico, and Uruguay, I’m proud of the frameworks—but I’m most proud of the people:
• Not just the processes.
• Not just the standards.
• Not just the governance.
<> The leaders who grew along the way.

I’ve always believed that great leaders are measured less by what they accomplish personally and more by the leaders they help develop around them. Watching teams take risks, build trusted partnerships, and prove that real influence comes from consistency and expertise rather than org charts has been the greatest joy of my career.

For those who worked with me over the decades, I hope a few of my "Bruce-isms" stuck. Remember that ... Hope is NOT a Strategy ... Quality isn't a phase, a gate, or a testing event—it’s everyone's responsibility ... Never settle, keep challenging the status quo, and never let someone else define what success looks like for you ... If something isn't working: challenge it, improve it, and don't be afraid to think differently.

As for me, I’m ready for the next chapter. I still have the same passion I've always had, only now I’m dedicating it to the things that make life fun and memorable—most importantly, sharing that time with my amazing wife, who supported me through every late-night deployment, production issue, and leadership challenge over the years.

To everyone across CIGNA, Bank of America, and Ahold Delhaize USA who shared this journey with me: thank you for the opportunities, the lessons, and the friendships.

The title changes, the calendar clears, and the next great adventure begins.
Keep moving forward! 🥂⛳️

Exactly on this day, I walked out of EY.

Not impulsively — I'd been preparing for this moment for 10 years. The dream of running my own company was always there. I just needed the discipline to get ready for it while still showing up at a 9-5.

That day, I went all-in on MBI ( M Brothers International) — a company actually founded back in 2015, but only now could give everything I had.

Since then, it's been a mix of wins and hard lessons.
We've worked with the Government of Tanzania, companies across the UK, USA, Ethiopia, Dubai, South Africa, and India — including delivering training to teams at Bank of America and IRIS Software, few more directly and through partners. 

We've also partnered with institutions like MIT Pune, D Y Patil, PCU, JSPM, LNCT Indore and others, giving 50+ students their first break through internships.

We've started building our own AI products too, moving from pure consulting into product thinking.

But not everything worked. We fought hard to win two ERP implementation bids with the Ethiopian Government. We lost both. Those losses taught me more than most of the wins combined.

Honestly, the hardest part isn't the work.
It's the balance. With a small kid at home, there's no boss pushing me anymore — just me, deciding every day how much to give to work and how much to give home.

10 years of preparation. One decision to leap. A journey still being written.
Grateful for everyone who's been part of it.

So United Airlines just told the world that AI agents can’t book its flights, not even with a human approving the purchase, and if you break the rule they can cancel your booking, wipe your miles and take away your status. Their reason is that agents are a risk to cybersecurity and undermine federal regulations. Full marks for vagueness, although the fine print is more honest about credential sharing. And the week before that, Bank of America was politely asking customers to please stop handing their passwords to their AI assistants.

In practice this means a login can no longer prove who’s actually acting. The other big one is liability. If an AI agent buys the wrong ticket or changes some account details, did the customer approve it? Nobody can say for sure, so every mistake turns into a dispute and a refund.

I totally get it. Their real problem is that they can’t tell a customer apart from an agent acting for that customer, because right now the agent turns up wearing the customer’s password. That would scare anyone, and you’d probably ban it too. But banning agents is really the 2026 version of banning smartphones in the office. People will use them anyway, they’ll just do it more quietly and with worse habits. So what are they really stopping?

And man, these agents can be crafty. US banks have been finding outside agents inside customer accounts doing things the customer never asked for. Because we instruct agents in natural language, there’s no fool-proof way to tell what was legitimate from what was overreach. No surprise the US bank regulator now puts fully autonomous payment agents in its highest risk tier.

The fix is fairly obvious if you think about it. Agents shouldn’t be borrowing a human’s login at all. They should carry their own identity, with authority that’s scoped to the task, capped, time-bound and revocable, and every action should leave a record the airline or the bank can check without having to take anyone’s word for it. Then nobody has to choose between blocking agents completely and trusting them blindly.

And the regulators are already heading exactly there. Hong Kong’s banking regulator launched a programme this month looking at precisely this: verifying an agent’s identity and the authority it’s been given before it’s allowed to transact.
Know your agents, verify everyone else’s, and prove what each one did. That’s the job, and it’s the one we’re doing at nonsudo.

PS: there’s also a commercial motive that no one is really talking about. An agent booking through United’s site means United loses a customer touchpoint, and with it the chance to sell upgrades and extras. Maybe they can pivot to upselling the agents. :D
